I've been farming these 5 mu for ten years now, and I know my land well. Here in Quzhou County, the wheat-maize rotation is what works best on the North China Plain. With my wife working part-time in town and my parents helping when they can, I can't afford to spend every day in the fields, so I need a practical plan that balances yield with the labor I have available.

For the winter wheat, I'll plant an improved high-yield variety in mid-October on all 5 mu. The soil here is decent but needs fertility, so I'll apply about 20 kg of nitrogen per mu, split between basal and top-dressing, plus 8 kg of phosphorus and 5 kg of potassium. Wheat needs water at critical stages, so I'll irrigate four times: at green-up, jointing, heading, and grain-filling. I'll do rotary tillage before sowing to break up the stubble and prepare a good seedbed. Three pesticide sprays should handle the main diseases and pests we usually see.

For the summer maize, I'll plant a hybrid variety right after the wheat harvest in early June — no time to waste. I can get away with lighter tillage after wheat, maybe rotary tillage or even minimal tillage if the stubble isn't too thick, since maize planting needs to happen fast before the season gets too hot. I'll apply around 18 kg nitrogen per mu, 6 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium. Maize here usually does okay with rainfall in summer, but the well gives me insurance, so I'll irrigate twice — once at the V6 stage and once at flowering if it doesn't rain. Two pesticide applications will keep the corn borer and leaf blight under control.

I expect the wheat to yield about 550 kg per mu, and the maize around 650 kg per mu. That's a solid, realistic target for my land.
